fatal_errors: The proposed Q235/Ti-modified CoCrFeNi laser-cladding system does not reconstruct the target SS316L/AlCoCrFeNi atmospheric-plasma-sprayed and 550 °C annealed system.
The proposed 25–150 °C NaCl exposures do not represent the target 3.5 wt% H2SO4 electrochemical test or 900 °C cyclic molten-salt hot-corrosion conditions.
No unmodified CoCrFeNi coating or Ti-content series is included, so the experiment cannot isolate Ti modification as the governing cause.

The cited evidence does not support corrosion performance at approximately 150 °C; E1 concerns 3.5 wt% NaCl without establishing that elevated-temperature boundary, while E2 concerns different HEA compositions and geothermal erosion-corrosion.
An aqueous 3.5 wt% NaCl test at 150 °C requires a specified pressurized test system and control of dissolved gases; the proposed corrosion-cell conditions are incomplete.
explanation: The hypothesis is scientifically plausible as an alternative centered on Q235 steel, and E1 directly supports studying laser-cladded CoCrFeNiTi_x coatings on Q235 in 3.5 wt% NaCl. It also provides an untreated reference, standard electrochemical and microscopy measurements, and a meaningful failure criterion. However, it has little agreement with the hidden target: substrate, coating chemistry, deposition process, annealing intervention, exposure media, elevated temperature, structural mediator, and quantitative outcomes all differ. Its mechanism is only generically similar through defect suppression and passive-film protection. The controlled study can establish whether the complete coating treatment improves corrosion resistance, but it cannot establish whether Ti, reduced defects, adhesion, or passive-film chemistry causes the improvement. Decisive mechanistic testing would require uncoated Q235, laser-processed Q235, unmodified CoCrFeNi, and multiple Ti levels, followed by coating-defect quantification and passive-film compositional analysis such as XPS or depth-resolved spectroscopy.
